analysis.one_liner: Gives consumers stronger rights over their credit reports, restricts prescreened offers, and regulates credit repair firms.
analysis.headline: Introduced in January 1993 with no cosponsors, the bill went to the House Banking Committee's consumer credit subcommittee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the Fair Credit Reporting Act, the law governing the private companies that compile credit files on Americans. Consumers would get the right to see everything in their file, have disputed errors reinvestigated free of charge, get a free copy of their report after being turned down for credit, and opt out of having their file sold for pre-approved credit offers and marketing. It would also require written consent before an employer pulls someone's credit report, bar medical information from credit files without consent, and impose the first federal rules on credit repair companies. At the same time, it would preempt state laws on credit reporting and lift the dollar thresholds that exempt large transactions from some rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers with errors in their credit files, people denied credit, insurance, jobs, or housing because of those errors, borrowers flooded with prescreened credit offers, and customers of credit repair scams. Disputing inaccurate information currently costs consumers time and often money; the bill would require free reinvestigation and deletion of information the bureau cannot verify, and free reports after an adverse decision [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires credit bureaus to disclose all information in a consumer's file, the identity of recent report recipients, and a written summary of the consumer's rights, with a toll-free number for nationwide bureaus [S2][S3].

Requires free reinvestigation of disputed information, deletion of anything inaccurate or unverifiable, and procedures preventing deleted errors from reappearing without certification of accuracy [S2][S3].

Gives consumers a free credit report within 60 days after an adverse action such as a credit denial, and requires anyone taking adverse action based on a credit score to disclose that the score was used and the principal factors behind it [S3].

Creates a nationwide toll-free notification system letting consumers exclude their name and address from lists sold for pre-screened credit and direct marketing offers, and restricts the information marketers can receive [S2][S3].

Bars employers from pulling a consumer report without written disclosure and consent, and requires giving the person a copy of the report and a chance to respond before taking adverse action [S2][S3].

Shortens how long minor late payments stay on a report (3 to 5 years depending on severity) and lets consumers exclude missed payments made while receiving unemployment compensation if the account is later brought current [S3].
Prohibits credit bureaus from maintaining or furnishing medical information without the consumer's consent, and from reporting missed payments on accounts the consumer closed, once notified [S3].

Extends civil liability for willful or negligent violations from bureaus and report users to any person, raises criminal penalties for obtaining information under false pretenses, and authorizes state attorneys general to sue violators in federal court [S2][S3].

Regulates credit repair companies for the first time federally: no advance fees before services are performed, written contracts, a 3-day right to cancel, bans on advising consumers to make false statements, and FTC enforcement with punitive damages and class actions available [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Consumer reporting agencies (credit bureaus) and the businesses that furnish information to them would bear new compliance costs: toll-free systems, dispute investigations, correction and update duties, prescreening opt-out administration, and expanded litigation exposure. Credit card issuers and direct marketers would face limits on prescreened solicitations. Lenders making large business transactions would benefit from raised exemption thresholds, while state-level rules would be wiped out by federal preemption [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit bureaus and data furnishing creditors

drawbacks.text: Section 118 would preempt 'any provision of the law of any State relating to the subject matter' of credit reporting, wiping out stronger state consumer reporting protections; the bill pairs new federal rights with a ceiling on state regulation, and blocks state court enforcement of the federal act while confining state actions to federal courts [S3].

The bill raises the exempted transaction thresholds from $50,000 to $200,000 for credit and insurance and from $20,000 to $100,000 for employment-related limits, removing large transactions from some reporting limits [S3].

New duties on companies that furnish information to bureaus—accuracy, corrections, and dispute investigation—would be enforced exclusively by federal agencies, with civil liability under the main enforcement sections expressly not applying to those duties [S3].
The bill would require credit bureaus to include overdue child support obligations in consumer reports, adding new negative information to consumers' files [S2][S3].

The prescreening opt-out election expires after two years unless the consumer renews it, and prescreened offers themselves remain permitted, so marketing based on credit files would continue with a notice-and-exit mechanism rather than a ban [S3].
The permitted fee for a credit report disclosure is set at up to $8 (inflation-adjusted), so routine access to one's own file would remain paid rather than free except after an adverse action [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill is a real gain for ordinary people: free reinvestigation of errors, free reports after denials, consent before employer background checks, and a way out of prescreened marketing, at a compliance cost borne by bureaus and creditors. But it is a bargain with a serious catch. The sweeping preemption of state law would trade stronger state-level protections and state courts for a single federal floor, and the raised exemption thresholds and carve-out from civil liability for data furnishers soften accountability exactly where much credit-report harm originates. Consumers who depend on aggressive state protections or private lawsuits would give up ground even as the federal baseline improved.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Banking Committee and then to its consumer credit subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Representative Al McCandless, a California Republican, introduced the Consumer Reporting Reform Act of 1993 on January 26, 1993 [S1][S2].
No other member cosponsored the bill [S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs on the day of introduction, and on February 12, 1993 to the Subcommittee on Consumer Credit and Insurance [S1][S5].
No further action appears in the record: the bill never received a subcommittee or committee vote, never reached the House floor, and died when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit bureaus, lenders, and direct marketers who sell and use consumer credit data are better off because the bill died: they continue operating under the older, weaker law with no federal duty to provide free post-denial reports, no consumer opt-out from prescreened lists, and no new accuracy or dispute duties. State-level rules remain unpreempted, but the stronger federal protections consumers would have gained never arrived.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit bureaus, lenders, and direct marketers

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 26, 1993; it was his only recorded action on it

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough to reveal a partisan split: it had a single Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no recorded votes or floor debate.

industries.note: The bill imposes real costs on bureaus—toll-free systems, full file disclosure, free post-denial reports, mandatory reinvestigation and deletion of unverifiable data—but its broad preemption of state law would lock in a single federal standard and shut out stricter state regimes, entrenching the three nationwide bureaus' position. Their interest in avoiding accuracy duties and liability runs against consumers' interest in accurate files.

industries.industry: Creditors and other furnishers of account data (banks, card issuers, collectors)
industries.note: Furnishers would face new duties to report complete, accurate information and to investigate disputes, though the bill shields those duties from private civil suits and enforces them only through federal agencies; raised exemption thresholds benefit lenders on large transactions. Their interest in reporting convenient information about borrowers runs against consumers' interest in accurate files.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and direct marketers using prescreened lists
industries.note: Prescreened solicitations would continue but marketers could receive only names and addresses, must disclose that credit file data was used, and must honor a toll-free consumer opt-out—cutting the pool of names available for mass mailings.

Title II bans advance fees, requires written contracts and disclosures, grants a 3-day cancellation right, and subjects the industry to FTC enforcement with punitive damages and class actions, targeting firms that profit from consumers with damaged credit.

industries.industry: Employment screening users of credit reports
industries.note: Employers would need written disclosure and consent to pull a report and must give the person a copy and a chance to respond before adverse action, raising the cost of screening workers by their credit histories.
